newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Nordic drink war fizzes as PepsiCo swops partners.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Nordic drink war fizzes as PepsiCo swops partners.

text.p: A battle of the beverages fizzed up again in the Nordic region on Tuesday after PepsiCo unveiled plans to ditch Swedish drinks partner Spendrups to join Norwegian-Swedish rival Pripps Ringnes.

The new partnership, to take effect from 2001, will create one of two major rival blocks in the region, competing against Coca-Cola which is currently awaiting approval for a proposed joint venture with Danish brewer Carlsberg.
The reshuffle leaves family-controlled Spendrups out in the cold, in danger of losing 20 percent of its turnover as PepsiCo deserts -- which analysts saw as an opening for another foreigner player.
"We are really surprised that Pepsi wants to end the cooperation in Sweden," Spendrup's managing director Jens Spendrup said in a statement on Tuesday.

"For more than a decade Pepsi has grown due to Spendrups' success. We will do everything in our power to defend this and other legal and economic rights that the company has in the current situation."
He said Spendrups had been under the impression that PepsiCo wanted to extend the cooperation beyond 2001.
The production, distribution and sales agreement between PepsiCo and Pripps Ringnes, owned by Norwegian conglomerate Orkla, concerns Sweden but the companies are also looking at Norway.
Analysts expected PepsiCo to reach an agreement in Finland with Hartwells to complete its Nordic coverage.

PepsiCo's plan to leave Spendrups when their current contract expires in 2001 sent Spendrups' share price tumbling on Tuesday -- despite the company posting a better than expected half year profit on Monday of 35 million crowns ($4.3 million).
At 1100 GMT it was trading three crowns lower at 56.5 crowns after falling as low as 54 crowns in early trade.
"The fall (was) a reaction to the cooperation statement," a Stockholm based analyst said. "But Spendrups told analysts this morning that this would not be the last word."
A Danish analyst said Spendrups would have to find a new partner to maintain some ground against its giant rivals.
"This announcement was negative for Spendrups which now definitely needs another partner," the analyst told Reuters. "It opens up the way for a foreign partner."
The Nordic battle of the beverages erupted in late 1995 when Coca-Cola cancelled a 43-year-old licensing deal with Pripps Ringnes, disappointed by falling market share.
After a public brawl, the two companies went behind closed doors to sort out their differences, finally announcing an official divorce in January this year.
Coca-Cola then proposed to Carlsberg and is currently awaiting a decision, due mid-September, from the European Commission on a joint Nordic bottling and distribution venture.
The venture would integrate the soft drink activities of Coca-Cola and Carlsberg, first in Denmark and Sweden and eventually in the whole of the Nordic and Baltic regions.
It also involves licence agreements and a distribution joint venture with the Swedish brewer Falcon, which is jointly owned by Carlsberg and the Finnish brewer Sinebrychoff.
The end of the deal with Coca-Cola threatened to wipe out a third of Pripps Ringnes annual turnover so it has welcomed cooperation with Pepsi which it said would last 20 years.
"Pepsi currently has about 15 percent of the soft drink" market, company spokesman Goran Orre told Reuters. "We expect to increase both market shares and volumes significantly."
The major advantage for Pepsi in Sweden is that Pripps Ringnes's distribution network covers 99 percent of retail outlets while Spendrup's coverage is 65 percent.
But Spendrups was not giving in without a fight.
"We are taking around one percent of the market share each year now and we will continue to do this in the future," Spendrup told Reuters.
